angle: 20 things rich people never buy, from 3 angles: numbers, psychology, playbook
title: 20 Things Rich People Never Buy

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. When people picture rich people, they picture them buying everything. The yacht, the watch, the car with the doors that open upward. But when researchers actually sat down with American millionaires and looked at their receipts, they found something strange. Most of them were quietly refusing to buy the very things the rest of us think we need. Today, twenty of those things.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's the number that started it all. In the book The Millionaire Next Door, researchers Thomas Stanley and William Danko surveyed American millionaires. Most of them said they had never spent more than three hundred ninety nine dollars on a suit.

card.label: most millionaires never paid more than
card.sub: for a suit (The Millionaire Next Door, 1996)

scenes.text: That book came out in nineteen ninety six, so prices have changed. But the pattern hasn't. Stanley kept studying millionaires for years after, and the same picture showed up again and again. The typical American millionaire is not a movie star or a tech founder. It's a business owner, a teacher, an engineer, a manager. Someone who earned a good income and simply refused to spend it all.
scenes.caption: THE QUIET MILLIONAIRE

scenes.text: And here's how this video works. We'll look at these twenty things from three angles. First, the numbers. What these purchases really cost over time. Second, the psychology. Why normal people buy them, and why rich people don't. And third, the playbook. What you can actually do differently, starting this week. By the end, you'll see that being rich is often less about what you buy, and more about what you refuse to buy.
scenes.caption: THREE ANGLES

scenes.text: Let's start with the cold, hard numbers. And number one is a purchase almost every American makes, usually more than once.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Every number in this video comes from a named source. Millionaire spending habits come from Thomas Stanley's research, including The Millionaire Next Door and Stop Acting Rich. Car prices come from Kelley Blue Book and Edmunds. Credit card rates come from the Federal Reserve. Growth examples use simple stated math, like a seven percent average yearly return. That's an illustration, not a promise. This is education, not financial advice.
scenes.caption: OUR SOURCES

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. These are the purchases where the math alone is enough to make a millionaire say no.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Number one. Rich people rarely buy a brand new car every few years.

card.title: Brand new cars, every few years
card.sub: the fastest way to lose money

scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 1
scenes.chapter: 1. Brand new cars, every few years

scenes.text: A new car starts losing value the moment you drive it home. Estimates from sources like Carfax and Edmunds put the drop at around twenty percent in the first year, and roughly half or more after five years, depending on the model. Meanwhile, Kelley Blue Book reported that the average price paid for a new vehicle in America passed fifty thousand dollars in twenty twenty five. That's a lot of money to watch melt.
scenes.caption: -20% IN YEAR ONE

scenes.text: In Stop Acting Rich, Stanley found that the median price millionaires paid for their most recent car was about thirty one thousand dollars, in a survey from the late two thousands. Many bought used, and many kept their cars for years. One of the most popular brands among them was Toyota, not Ferrari. Try this: before your next car, look up the five year resale value of the model. If it loses half, you're paying for that loss every month.
scenes.caption: RICH PEOPLE DRIVE TOYOTAS

scenes.text: Here's what that difference can grow into. Say you skip a car payment upgrade and invest three hundred dollars a month instead. At a seven percent average yearly return, over twenty years that's roughly one hundred fifty six thousand dollars.
Number two. Rich people don't pay credit card interest.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 2

scenes.text: According to the Federal Reserve, the average interest rate on credit card accounts that actually paid interest was above twenty percent in recent years. Think about what that means. If you carry a balance, every hundred dollar purchase can cost you more than one hundred twenty dollars by the end of the year. You're paying a premium on everything you buy.
scenes.caption: 20%+ INTEREST

scenes.text: Many wealthy people use credit cards. They just pay the full balance every month, so the card is a payment tool, not a loan. Some collect the rewards, which means the card company is paying them, not the other way around. Try this: open your last statement and find the line that says interest charged. Multiply it by twelve. That's what your balance is costing you a year.
scenes.caption: PAY IN FULL

scenes.text: Number three. Lottery tickets.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 3

scenes.text: Americans spend more than one hundred billion dollars a year on lottery tickets, according to the North American Association of State and Provincial Lotteries. The odds of winning the Powerball jackpot are about one in two hundred ninety two million. You are far more likely to be struck by lightning than to hit that jackpot.
scenes.caption: 1 IN 292 MILLION

scenes.text: On average, lotteries pay back only a portion of what players spend, which is how states raise money from them. So, on average, every ticket loses money. Rich people do take risks, but they take risks where the odds are on their side, like owning businesses and investments. Try this: if you buy tickets, add up what you spent last year. Then imagine that money in an index fund instead.
scenes.caption: LIGHTNING IS MORE LIKELY

scenes.text: Number four. Extended warranties on small electronics.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 4

scenes.text: When you buy a television or a laptop, the checkout screen often offers an extended warranty. Stores push these hard because they're profitable. Consumer Reports has long argued that most of them aren't worth the money, because many products don't break during the coverage period, and many credit cards already add some extra warranty protection.
scenes.caption: PROFIT FOR THE STORE

scenes.text: Wealthy people think about insurance differently. They insure against disasters they can't afford, like a house fire or a lawsuit. They don't insure against losses they could easily pay for, like a broken blender. Instead, they self insure, keeping cash ready for small surprises. Try this: next time you're offered a warranty, ask yourself, could I replace this item without hurting my budget? If yes, skip it.
scenes.caption: SELF INSURE

scenes.text: Number five. Timeshares.

card.title: Timeshares
card.sub: easy to buy, hard to sell

scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 5

scenes.text: A timeshare lets you buy the right to use a vacation property for a week or so each year. The sales pitch is usually a free trip or a free dinner, followed by a long presentation. The price can easily run into the tens of thousands of dollars, and there are yearly maintenance fees on top that tend to rise over time.
scenes.caption: THE FREE TRIP PITCH

scenes.text: The real problem shows up when you want out. The resale market for timeshares is weak, and many owners find they can sell only for a small fraction of what they paid, if they can sell at all. The Federal Trade Commission even warns about timeshare resale scams. Rich people prefer flexibility. They rent the vacation they want, when they want it. Try this: if you're tempted, look up the resale listings for the same resort first.
scenes.caption: HARD TO SELL

scenes.text: Number six. More house than they need.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 6

scenes.text: A bigger house doesn't just mean a bigger mortgage. It means bigger property taxes, bigger insurance, bigger heating and cooling bills, more furniture, more repairs, and more maintenance, every year, for as long as you live there. A common rule of thumb is to budget around one to two percent of a home's value each year just for upkeep.
scenes.caption: BIGGER EVERY BILL

scenes.text: Stanley's research found that many millionaires lived in homes far below what they could afford. One of the most famous examples is Warren Buffett, who still lives in the house in Omaha he bought in nineteen fifty eight for about thirty one thousand five hundred dollars. Try this: add up everything your home really costs per month, not just the mortgage. Taxes, insurance, utilities and repairs. That's your real housing cost.
scenes.caption: BUFFETT'S HOUSE SINCE 1958

scenes.text: Number seven. Fees they can avoid.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 7

scenes.text: Overdraft fees, ATM fees, late fees, high fund fees, account maintenance fees. Each one looks tiny. But together they can add up to hundreds of dollars a year. And investment fees are the sneakiest, because a one percent yearly fee on a growing balance can cost tens of thousands of dollars over a lifetime of investing.
scenes.caption: FEES ADD UP

scenes.text: Rich people are almost allergic to fees. They read the fee schedule. They move their money to banks that don't charge for basics. They choose low cost funds. They pay bills on time, often with automatic payments, so late fees never happen. Try this: go through the last three months of bank statements and circle every fee. Then make one phone call or one switch to stop the biggest one.
scenes.caption: CIRCLE EVERY FEE

scenes.text: Before we move to the psychology, one more piece of math that ties all seven together. A dollar you don't spend is often worth more than a dollar you earn. Here's why. When you earn an extra dollar, taxes take a piece first. Federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare, and in many places state tax too. Depending on your bracket, you might keep seventy or eighty cents of it.
scenes.caption: TAXES COME FIRST
scenes.chapter: A dollar saved beats a dollar earned

scenes.text: But when you avoid spending a dollar, you keep the whole dollar. So cutting a one hundred dollar monthly fee or interest charge can be worth as much as a raise of well over one hundred dollars a month before taxes. That's why wealthy people take boring costs so seriously. Cutting a cost is like getting a raise that nobody can take away, and you don't have to ask your boss for it.
scenes.caption: A RAISE YOU GIVE YOURSELF

scenes.text: And there's a second layer. Money you don't spend can be invested, and the growth on that money can compound for decades. So every one of these seven refusals has a triple effect. You keep the full dollar. You avoid the loss that comes with the purchase. And you gain the future growth. Add those three together over a working lifetime, and you start to understand how ordinary earners become quiet millionaires.
scenes.caption: THE TRIPLE EFFECT

scenes.text: So that's angle one. The numbers. Notice something? None of these are about being cheap. They're about not paying for things that make someone else rich at your expense. Now angle two, the psychology. Because the numbers alone don't explain why smart people keep buying these things.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's the uncomfortable truth. Most people know a new car loses value. Most people know lottery odds are terrible. They buy anyway. Why? Because spending isn't really a math decision. It's an emotional one. It's about status, comfort, belonging and fear. The next seven things on our list are the ones rich people skip because they've learned to see the psychology behind them.
scenes.caption: SPENDING IS EMOTIONAL

scenes.text: Number eight. Status symbols.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 8

scenes.text: Stanley described a type of person he called the income statement affluent. People with high incomes who look rich, with the big house, the luxury car and the designer clothes, but who have little actual wealth. Their money goes out as fast as it comes in. He contrasted them with the balance sheet affluent, who might look ordinary but own real assets.
scenes.caption: LOOKING RICH

scenes.text: The trap is that status purchases are designed to be seen. And once you buy one, your new neighbors and coworkers have the same things, so the status fades and you need the next one. Economists call this keeping up with the Joneses. Try this: before a big purchase, ask, would I still buy this if nobody could ever see it? If the answer is no, you're paying for an audience.
scenes.query: Neighbors houses with cars in driveways
scenes.caption: KEEPING UP WITH THE JONESES

scenes.text: Number nine. Designer labels for the sake of the label.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 9

scenes.text: Remember the numbers from The Millionaire Next Door. Most millionaires surveyed had never spent more than three hundred ninety nine dollars on a suit, one hundred forty dollars on shoes, or two hundred thirty five dollars on a wristwatch. Those were nineteen nineties dollars, so adjust for inflation, but the point stands. Most of them simply didn't care about labels.
scenes.caption: $399 SUIT, $235 WATCH

scenes.text: This doesn't mean rich people buy junk. Many buy good quality items and use them for years. The difference is that they pay for quality, not for a logo. A plain, well made coat that lasts ten years is cheaper than a fashionable one that lasts two. Try this: look at the five most expensive pieces in your closet. How often do you actually wear them? Divide the price by the number of times worn.
scenes.caption: QUALITY, NOT LOGOS

scenes.text: Number ten. The newest phone the day it comes out.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 10

scenes.text: Flagship phones can cost a thousand dollars or more. Upgrading every year, often through a monthly payment plan, makes that cost feel small. But each new model usually brings modest improvements over the last one. Many people pay full price for features they never use.
scenes.caption: $1,000 EVERY YEAR

scenes.text: The psychology here is novelty. Your brain gets a little reward from something new and shiny, and companies schedule launches to trigger exactly that. Many wealthy people keep their devices until they actually stop working well. Try this: when the next launch comes, write down three specific things your current phone can't do that you actually need. If you can't find three, wait a year.
scenes.caption: USE IT UNTIL IT DIES

scenes.text: Number eleven. Things bought to impress strangers online.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 11

scenes.text: Social media turned everyone's life into a highlight reel. You see the vacation, the new kitchen, the car. You don't see the credit card bill. Surveys from groups like Bankrate and Credit Karma have found that a meaningful share of younger adults say they've overspent because of something they saw on social media.
scenes.caption: THE HIGHLIGHT REEL

scenes.text: Rich people are often remarkably private about money. Stanley's millionaires valued financial independence over social display. If you're not trying to impress anyone, you're free to spend on what you actually enjoy. Try this: unfollow five accounts that make you want to buy things. Notice how your wants change in the next month.
scenes.caption: UNFOLLOW FIVE

scenes.text: Quick pause. If you're getting value from this, do me a favor and subscribe to Ryan Rover Money. It's free, it helps the channel a lot, and every week we break down how money really works, with real numbers. Okay, back to the psychology. Number twelve is one that hits close to home for a lot of people.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Number twelve. Convenience at any price.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 12

scenes.text: Delivery fees, service fees, tips, and marked up menu prices can make a delivered meal cost much more than the same food picked up or cooked at home. Doing it once is fine. Doing it every day quietly becomes one of the biggest lines in a budget, and most people never add it up.
scenes.caption: THE CONVENIENCE TAX

scenes.text: Wealthy people do pay for convenience, but deliberately. They might pay for help with something that saves them hours, like a big home repair, while still cooking simple meals most nights. The rule is intention. Try this: check your delivery app history for the last month and add up the total, including fees and tips. Then decide what that number should be next month.
scenes.caption: CHOOSE ON PURPOSE

scenes.text: Number thirteen. Retail therapy.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 13

scenes.text: Buying something can lift your mood for a moment. Researchers have studied this, and shopping can genuinely make people feel better in the short term. The problem is that the feeling fades quickly, and the bill doesn't. Over time, using shopping to manage stress can become an expensive habit.
scenes.caption: A MOOD, NOT A NEED

scenes.text: Many rich people have replaced spending with cheaper ways to feel good. Walking, exercise, reading, time with friends. Not because they're saints, but because they noticed the difference between a purchase that adds value and one that just covers a bad day. Try this: use a twenty four hour rule. If you want something that isn't essential, put it in the cart and wait a day. Often, the urge passes.
scenes.caption: THE 24 HOUR RULE

scenes.text: Number fourteen. Financial products they don't understand.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 14

scenes.text: Some investment products are sold with complicated features, guarantees and fine print. Some of them come with high fees and long lock up periods, with penalties to get out early. The complexity isn't always there to help the buyer. Sometimes it's there to hide the cost.
scenes.caption: IF IT'S CONFUSING, CAREFUL

scenes.text: Warren Buffett has famously said he only invests in businesses he understands. Many wealthy people follow a version of that rule. If they can't explain how a product makes money and what it costs, they don't buy it. Try this: if someone pitches you an investment, ask three questions. How do you get paid? What are all the fees? How do I get my money out? If the answers are vague, walk away.
scenes.caption: ONLY WHAT YOU UNDERSTAND

scenes.text: That's angle two. Status, novelty, convenience, emotion, complexity. Rich people feel all of those pulls too. They've just learned to notice them. Now the best part. Angle three. The playbook. What do rich people buy instead, and how can you copy it?
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's the shift. Rich people don't just avoid things. They redirect the money toward things that grow. Every item in this last group is something they refuse to buy, paired with what they buy instead. That pairing is the whole playbook.
scenes.caption: REDIRECT THE MONEY

scenes.text: Number fifteen. Lifestyle upgrades before they own assets.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 15

scenes.text: A common pattern among people who build wealth is a simple order of operations. First, they build income producing assets, like retirement accounts, index funds, a business or rental property. Then, once those assets are growing, they use part of the growth for lifestyle upgrades. Most people do it the other way around.
scenes.caption: ASSETS FIRST

scenes.text: Think about a raise. Most people upgrade their lifestyle the same month. Many wealthy people save the first raise, or at least half of it, before anything else changes. That way their spending never catches up to their income. Try this: next time you get a raise, set up an automatic transfer of half the increase into investments before your first new paycheck arrives.
scenes.caption: SAVE HALF THE RAISE

scenes.text: Number sixteen. Cheap tools that break, over and over.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 16

scenes.text: This one surprises people. Rich people often refuse to buy the cheapest version of things they use every day. A very cheap pair of boots that falls apart every year can cost more over ten years than a well made pair that lasts a decade. The writer Terry Pratchett called this the boots theory of poverty.
scenes.caption: BUY ONCE, CRY ONCE

scenes.text: The key is the word every day. For things you use constantly, like a mattress, work shoes, a reliable car or good kitchen knives, quality can save money. For things you use once a year, cheap is fine. Try this: list the five things you use most. Are any of them cheap replacements you keep buying? That's where quality pays.
scenes.caption: QUALITY FOR DAILY USE

scenes.text: Number seventeen. Complex insurance they don't need.

card.title: Whole life policies they don't need

scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 17
scenes.chapter: 17. Whole life policies they don't need

scenes.text: Life insurance matters if people depend on your income. But some policies mix insurance with investing, and they can carry high costs. Many personal finance experts suggest that most families are well served by simple term life insurance, which covers a set number of years for a much lower premium.
scenes.caption: PROTECT THE FAMILY

scenes.text: The principle is to keep insurance and investing separate, so you can see what each one costs. Buy the coverage you need, compare quotes, and invest the difference in low cost accounts. Some people do have reasons for permanent policies, so this is a question to ask a fee only advisor about, not a rule for everyone. Try this: find your current policy and write down what you pay each year and what it covers.
scenes.caption: KNOW WHAT YOU PAY

scenes.text: Number eighteen. Brand name basics.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 18

scenes.text: Store brand groceries, medicines and household products are often made to similar standards as the name brands, and can cost noticeably less. For over the counter medicines, the active ingredient is listed on the label, and the store version often has exactly the same one. The difference is mostly packaging and advertising.
scenes.caption: SAME INSIDE, LESS COST

scenes.text: Researchers in Chicago once studied shoppers and found that pharmacists and doctors were much more likely to buy store brand headache medicine than other shoppers. When people know what's inside the box, they stop paying for the brand. Try this: on your next grocery trip, swap five name brand items for store brands. If you can't tell the difference, keep the swap.
scenes.caption: WHAT EXPERTS BUY

scenes.text: Number nineteen. Subscriptions they don't use.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 19

scenes.text: Streaming services, apps, gym memberships, boxes delivered every month. Each one costs a few dollars, and many renew automatically. Surveys regularly find that people underestimate how much they spend on subscriptions, sometimes by a wide margin. The business model depends on you forgetting.
scenes.caption: THE QUIET LEAK

scenes.text: Rich people treat recurring costs as serious, because a recurring cost is like a reverse investment. Fifteen dollars a month for ten years is eighteen hundred dollars, before you count what that money could have earned. Try this: search your bank and card statements for every charge that repeats. Cancel anything you haven't used in the last thirty days. You can always sign up again.
scenes.caption: CANCEL WHAT YOU DON'T USE

scenes.text: And number twenty. Deals that waste their time.
scenes.caption: NEVER BUY 20

scenes.text: This is the twist ending. Rich people don't chase every coupon or drive across town to save two dollars. Time is the one thing nobody can buy more of. A deal that costs an hour to save a few dollars is often a bad trade, and buying things just because they're on sale isn't saving at all. It's spending.
scenes.caption: TIME IS MONEY

scenes.text: The wealthy focus on the big decisions, where the real money is. Housing, cars, taxes, fees and investing. Get those five right, and you can relax about the price of coffee. Get them wrong, and no amount of coupon clipping will save you. Try this: rank your five biggest yearly expenses. Spend your energy cutting the top one, not the smallest one.
scenes.query: House and car keys on table
scenes.caption: WIN THE BIG FIVE

scenes.text: Before we wrap up the three angles, let me tell you a story. It's made up, but it's built from the patterns Stanley found again and again.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Meet two neighbors on the same street. Mark is a sales director earning two hundred thousand dollars a year. Linda is a high school teacher married to an electrician, and together they earn about one hundred thirty thousand dollars. From the street, Mark looks like the rich one. He has the bigger house, a new luxury SUV every three years, and a boat in the driveway.
scenes.query: Two houses side by side street
scenes.caption: TWO NEIGHBORS

scenes.text: Linda and her husband drive a ten year old minivan and a pickup truck they bought used. Their house is smaller and paid down fast. They cook most meals, take one simple vacation a year, and since their first jobs they have put fifteen percent of their pay into retirement accounts and index funds, automatically, every single month.
scenes.caption: THE ORDINARY ONES

scenes.text: Twenty five years later, Mark has a big income, a big mortgage and a big car loan. If he lost his job, his family could last maybe three months. Linda and her husband have a paid off house and investments that, at historical average returns, could plausibly be well over a million dollars. They could stop working tomorrow. Mark can't stop for a single month.
scenes.caption: 25 YEARS LATER

scenes.text: Stanley's research suggested this pattern was common. He found that, among high income households, the ones who accumulated the most wealth were usually the ones who spent the least on visible status items. Income makes you look rich. Wealth makes you free. And the twenty things on this list are exactly where that difference gets decided.
scenes.caption: LOOKING RICH VS BEING FREE

scenes.text: Now let's put the three angles together, because this is where it gets exciting.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: What the skipped purchases add up to

scenes.text: Imagine someone who skips just a few of these. They keep their car a few years longer instead of upgrading. They pay their credit card in full. They cancel two subscriptions they don't use and cut back on delivery. It's not hard to imagine that freeing up five hundred dollars a month for a typical household. Not by living in misery. Just by refusing to pay for things that don't add much to their life.
scenes.caption: $500 A MONTH

scenes.text: Now invest that five hundred dollars a month at a seven percent average yearly return. After thirty years, that could grow to roughly six hundred ten thousand dollars. You would have put in one hundred eighty thousand. The rest is growth.

That's the secret Stanley kept finding in his research. The millionaire next door didn't get there through one big win. They got there by quietly refusing hundreds of small and medium purchases, and putting that money to work for decades. It's not exciting. It's not glamorous. But it works for ordinary people with ordinary incomes, and that's what makes it powerful.
scenes.caption: QUIET REFUSALS

scenes.text: So if rich people refuse all these things, what do they actually spend on? Because they do spend. They just spend differently.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: What rich people do spend on

scenes.text: First, they buy time. Many wealthy people will happily pay for things that free up hours, like help with a big project, or living close to work to avoid a two hour commute. Time saved can go into a business, a skill, their health or their family. That's spending that pays them back.
scenes.caption: THEY BUY TIME

scenes.text: Second, they buy knowledge. Books, courses, coaching, conferences in their field. Stanley noticed that many of the millionaires he studied were serious about learning and about investing in their children's education. A skill that raises your income for the rest of your career can be the best return you'll ever get.
scenes.caption: THEY BUY KNOWLEDGE

scenes.text: Third, they buy health. Good food, exercise, preventive care, sleep. Health problems are one of the biggest financial risks a family faces, and medical bills are a leading reason people fall behind. Spending a little on staying healthy is protecting your biggest asset, which is your ability to work and enjoy life.
scenes.caption: THEY BUY HEALTH

scenes.text: Fourth, they buy assets. Index funds, retirement accounts, a share of a business, a rental property. Things that tend to grow or pay income over time. And fifth, they buy experiences with the people they love. Research on happiness has often suggested that experiences, especially shared ones, bring more lasting satisfaction than things. A camping trip with your kids can stay with you longer than a new couch.
scenes.caption: ASSETS AND EXPERIENCES

scenes.text: Notice the pattern. Time, knowledge, health, assets and relationships. Every one of them either grows in value or makes your life better for years. Compare that with the twenty things on our list, which mostly lose value the moment you pay. That's the real difference between how rich people and everyone else spend.
scenes.caption: SPEND ON WHAT GROWS

scenes.text: Now, a challenge. Let's make this practical with a thirty day experiment.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Week one, the numbers. Pull up your last three months of statements. Highlight every fee, every interest charge, and every payment on something that loses value, like a car loan. Don't change anything yet. Just see the total. Most people are surprised by it, and that surprise is useful.
scenes.caption: WEEK 1: SEE IT

scenes.text: Week two, the psychology. Every time you want to buy something that isn't essential, write it down with the reason. Was it boredom? Stress? Something you saw online? Something a friend has? Don't judge yourself. Just name it. By the end of the week, you'll see your own patterns clearly.
scenes.caption: WEEK 2: NAME IT

scenes.text: Week three, the playbook. Make three changes. Cancel the subscriptions you don't use. Call to remove one fee or lower one interest rate. And set up one automatic transfer into savings or investments on payday, even if it's small. Twenty five dollars counts. The habit matters more than the amount.
scenes.caption: WEEK 3: CHANGE IT

scenes.text: Week four, redirect. Take whatever you freed up and point it at something that grows. Your emergency fund first, if you don't have one. Then high interest debt. Then long term investing. At the end of thirty days, you'll have a number you can see, and that number is your proof that this works for you, not just for millionaires in a book.
scenes.caption: WEEK 4: REDIRECT IT

scenes.text: Three mistakes people make when they try this. Mistake one, going too extreme. If you cut every pleasure at once, you'll burn out and swing back to spending. Keep a small budget for fun, guilt free. Mistake two, comparing yourself with others. Your plan only has to beat your old habits, not your neighbor.
scenes.caption: DON'T GO TOO EXTREME

scenes.text: Mistake three, saving without a destination. Money that just sits in a checking account tends to get spent. Give every freed up dollar a job, whether that's an emergency fund, a debt payoff, or an investment account. When money has a job, it's much harder to waste.
scenes.caption: GIVE EVERY DOLLAR A JOB

scenes.text: Let me answer a few questions people always ask about this topic.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Question one. Isn't this just being cheap? No. Being cheap means always choosing the lowest price, even when it costs you more later, or costs your relationships. Being frugal means spending deliberately on what you value and cutting what you don't. Many wealthy people spend generously on education, health, travel or family. They just don't spend on autopilot.
scenes.caption: CHEAP VS FRUGAL

scenes.text: Question two. But don't rich people buy luxury things? Some do, of course. The people you see on television and social media often do. But Stanley's research suggests that the typical millionaire, the one you'd never notice, lives well below their means. The flashy minority gets all the attention. The quiet majority gets the wealth.
scenes.caption: THE FLASHY MINORITY

scenes.text: Question three. I don't earn much. Does any of this matter for me? It matters even more. When money is tight, every fee, every point of interest and every unused subscription takes a bigger bite. And the habits you build at a small income are the ones that carry you when your income grows. Start with the one item on this list that costs you the most.
scenes.caption: SMALL INCOME, BIG IMPACT

scenes.text: Question four. Should I sell my new car right now? Not necessarily. Selling a car you just bought often locks in the biggest part of the loss. For many people, the better move is to keep it, take good care of it, pay it off, and then drive it for years after the last payment. That payment free stretch is where the real savings live.
scenes.caption: KEEP IT LONGER

scenes.text: Question six. What about my partner? What if they love spending? This is common, and it's a conversation, not a battle. Sit down together and agree on a few big goals first, like a house, an emergency fund or retiring early. Then give each person a personal spending amount, no questions asked. Couples who share goals usually find it much easier to cut what doesn't matter.
scenes.caption: TALK WITH YOUR PARTNER

scenes.text: Question seven. Is it ever okay to buy a nice car or a designer item? Of course. The question is order and proportion. If your emergency fund is full, your debt is handled, and you're investing steadily, a treat you truly love is your choice. Many wealthy people do have one or two splurges. They just choose them on purpose, and they pay cash.
scenes.caption: SPLURGE ON PURPOSE

scenes.text: Question eight. How long until I see results? The savings show up in your account the very first month you cut a fee or cancel a subscription. The bigger results take longer. Compounding is slow at the start and fast at the end, so the first few years can feel like nothing is happening. Keep going anyway. Most people who quit, quit right before the curve starts bending upward.
scenes.caption: HOW LONG IT TAKES

scenes.text: And question five. Where do I start? Pick one item from each angle. One from the numbers, like credit card interest. One from the psychology, like status purchases. One from the playbook, like canceling unused subscriptions. Three small changes this month. That's how every money story that ends well actually starts.
scenes.caption: ONE FROM EACH ANGLE

scenes.text: Quick recap. Angle one, the numbers. Rich people never buy new cars every few years, never pay credit card interest, skip lottery tickets, extended warranties and timeshares, avoid too much house, and avoid fees.
scenes.caption: THE NUMBERS: 1 TO 7

scenes.text: Angle two, the psychology. They skip status symbols, designer labels, the newest phone every year, things to impress strangers, convenience at any price, retail therapy and financial products they don't understand.
scenes.caption: THE PSYCHOLOGY: 8 TO 14

scenes.text: Angle three, the playbook. No upgrades before assets, no cheap tools that break, no complex insurance they don't need, no brand name basics, no unused subscriptions, and no deals that waste their time.
scenes.caption: THE PLAYBOOK: 15 TO 20

scenes.caption: RYAN
